summary: One headline figure and how it moved against a comparison period. Good and bad come from `goodWhen`, never from the sign alone.
useWhen: a dashboard or overview leads with a handful of key numbers
a change against a previous period is part of what the number means

useInstead.when: it is a summary with text and media rather than a number
the figure is progress toward a known total
there are more than about six figures, or they need comparing across rows

composition.note: Always inside a StatGroup: the tile renders a <dt> and a <dd>, which are only valid inside a <dl>.

up.use: the default — revenue, success rate, anything where more is better

down.use: costs, durations, error counts and queues, where a rise is bad news

neutral.use: a change that is neither — run volume, traffic — so it is never coloured

points.use: the metric is itself a percentage: 95% to 96% is +1.0 pts, not +1.1%

guarantees: the verdict is spoken as text ("better" or "worse") after the change, so it never rests on the badge's colour
the direction is in the text as a sign as well as in the arrow
`isLoading` marks the tile aria-busy while its placeholder shows
requires: `value` already formatted — the tile cannot know the locale, precision or unit
the right `goodWhen` for the metric; the default `up` colours a rising cost green

antiPatterns.dont: leaving `goodWhen` at `up` for a duration, cost or error count
antiPatterns.why: a slower, costlier or more error-prone week is shown green and announced as better

antiPatterns.dont: a percentage change for a metric that is already a percentage
antiPatterns.why: 95% to 96% is +1 point; +1.1% misreports it — use changeUnit="points"

antiPatterns.dont: passing a change of 0 to mean "no data"
antiPatterns.why: 0 renders "No change", a claim; omit `change` when there is nothing to compare
